description: CISSP concepts across the 8 (ISC)² domains, each anchored with a short cloud/Kubernetes example. For cloud and platform architects preparing for the CISSP exam who want the theory to map onto real platforms.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: CIA triad: {{c1::confidentiality}}: prevent unauthorized disclosure; {{c2::integrity}}: prevent unauthorized alteration; {{c3::availability}}: timely, reliable access for authorized users.
notes.extra: K8s: etcd encryption + TLS (C); signed, immutable images (I); PodDisruptionBudgets and multi-cluster failover (A).

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: DAD triad: what does each letter stand for, and which CIA property does it defeat?
notes.back: Disclosure → confidentiality; Alteration → integrity; Destruction/Denial → availability.
notes.extra: The attacker's view of CIA. K8s: a Secret leaked via an over-permissive ServiceAccount = disclosure.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: What is non-repudiation, and what typically provides it?
notes.back: The originator can't later deny creating or sending something. Provided by digital signatures (only they hold the private key).
notes.extra: K8s: a cosign-signed image: the build pipeline can't deny producing it.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: What is authenticity (beyond CIA)?
notes.back: Assurance that data or a subject genuinely comes from its claimed source.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: Due diligence vs due care?
notes.back: Due diligence: investigate and understand risk ("do detect"). Due care: act prudently on it, implementing and maintaining controls ("do correct").
notes.analogy: Diligence is the home inspection; care is actually fixing the faulty wiring it found.
notes.extra: K8s: running kube-bench/Trivy = diligence; fixing findings and enforcing policy = care.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: Quantitative risk: SLE = {{c1::asset value × exposure factor}}; ALE = {{c2::SLE × ARO}} (annualized rate of occurrence).
notes.extra: K8s: cluster outage, AV €500k, EF 20% → SLE €100k; ARO 0.5 → ALE €50k/yr.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: Quantitatively, when is a control worth buying?
notes.back: When ALE<sub>before</sub> − ALE<sub>after</sub> − annual control cost > 0.
notes.extra: E.g. ALE drops €50k → €5k; a €20k/yr multi-cluster HA setup is justified.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: Risk responses: {{c1::mitigate}} (reduce with controls), {{c2::transfer}} (insurance, contracts), {{c3::avoid}} (stop the activity), {{c4::accept}} (formally tolerate).
notes.extra: K8s: a managed Kubernetes service shifts control-plane risk to the provider; workload, config and data risk stay with you.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: What is residual risk, and who must accept it?
notes.back: Risk remaining after controls; it must be formally accepted by senior management (the risk owner).

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: On the CISSP exam, is risk rejection (ignoring a risk) a valid response?
notes.back: No. Ignoring or denying a risk is never acceptable; only documented acceptance is.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: Qualitative vs quantitative risk analysis?
notes.back: Quantitative: money and probabilities (SLE/ALE); objective but data-hungry. Qualitative: relative ratings (high/medium/low, risk matrix); fast, subjective.
notes.extra: Most programs are hybrid. K8s: risk register ratings like "cluster-admin sprawl: likelihood medium, impact high".

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: What is the Delphi technique?
notes.back: Anonymous, iterative expert rating rounds that converge on a consensus while avoiding groupthink.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: STRIDE: {{c1::Spoofing::S}}, {{c2::Tampering::T}}, {{c3::Repudiation::R}}, {{c4::Information disclosure::I}}, {{c5::Denial of service::D}}, {{c6::Elevation of privilege::E}}.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: STRIDE threat → property violated: spoofing → {{c1::authenticity}}; tampering → {{c2::integrity}}; repudiation → non-repudiation; information disclosure → confidentiality; DoS → availability; elevation of privilege → {{c3::authorization}}.
notes.extra: K8s: spoofed kubelet identity, tampered etcd, leaked Secrets, privileged-container escape.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: Governance documents: policy (mandatory, high-level intent) → {{c1::standard}} (mandatory, specific requirements) → {{c2::procedure}} (mandatory, step-by-step). A {{c3::guideline}} is recommended, not mandatory.
notes.extra: K8s: policy-as-code turns a standard ("images must be signed") into an enforced Kyverno ClusterPolicy in Git.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: What is a security baseline?
notes.back: A minimum mandatory security configuration for a class of systems (e.g. a CIS Benchmark level).

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: Control functions: preventive, detective, corrective, deterrent, recovery, {{c1::compensating}} (alternative when the primary control is infeasible), {{c2::directive}} (mandates behaviour).

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: Classify by function: NetworkPolicy = {{c1::preventive}}; Falco alert = {{c2::detective}}; ArgoCD self-heal reverting drift = {{c3::corrective}}; Velero restore = {{c4::recovery}}.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: By type, controls are {{c1::administrative}}, {{c2::technical (logical)}} or {{c3::physical}}.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: What is defense in depth?
notes.back: Layering diverse, overlapping controls so no single failure compromises the system.
notes.analogy: A castle: moat, walls, gatehouse and keep. Breaching one still leaves the next.
notes.extra: K8s: cloud network → NetworkPolicy → Pod Security Admission → RBAC → seccomp/AppArmor → encrypted etcd → Falco.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: What is supply chain risk management (SCRM)?
notes.back: Managing risk introduced by third parties (vendors, hardware, software dependencies, service providers) via contracts, supplier baselines and assessments.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: Which artifacts support software supply-chain assurance, and what does each answer?
notes.back: SBOM: what's inside. Provenance attestation (SLSA): how and where it was built. Signature: who produced it.
notes.extra: K8s: enforce signature + provenance at admission; Harbor tag immutability.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: What does a Business Impact Analysis (BIA) produce?
notes.back: The critical processes and how disruption impact grows over time, from which MTD, RTO and RPO are set.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: {{c1::RTO}} (recovery time objective) = max time to restore service; {{c2::RPO}} (recovery point objective) = max acceptable data loss, measured in time.
notes.analogy: RPO is how long ago your last save point was; RTO is how long until you're playing again.
notes.extra: K8s: continuous WAL archiving (CloudNativePG) → RPO of seconds; nightly Velero backups → RPO up to 24 h.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: Continuity timing rule: {{c1::RTO + WRT (work recovery time)}} must fit within {{c2::MTD (maximum tolerable downtime)}}.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: What is the EU NIS2 Directive, and how does it bind an organization?
notes.back: Cybersecurity risk-management and incident-reporting duties for "essential" and "important" entities. As a directive, it binds via national transposition law.
notes.extra: NL: the Cyberbeveiligingswet.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.text: NIS2 incident reporting: early warning within {{c1::24 hours}}, incident notification within {{c2::72 hours}}, final report within one month.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::01 Security & Risk Management
notes.front: Under NIS2, who is personally accountable for cybersecurity risk management?
notes.back: The entity's management body: it must approve measures, oversee them and be trained, and can be held liable.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.text: Data roles: {{c1::owner}}: accountable, sets classification; {{c2::custodian}}: day-to-day technical protection (backups, permissions); {{c3::steward}}: data quality and business context.
notes.analogy: The owner decides what goes in the safe; the custodian holds the keys and keeps it locked.
notes.extra: K8s: the platform team is typically the custodian.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.text: GDPR roles: the {{c1::controller}} determines purposes and means of processing; the {{c2::processor}} processes on its behalf; the {{c3::subject}} is the person the data is about.
notes.extra: A public cloud provider is your processor, hence Data Processing Agreements and sub-processor lists.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.text: Data lifecycle: create → {{c1::store}} → use → {{c2::share}} → archive → {{c3::destroy}}.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.front: In the data lifecycle, when is classification assigned, and why then?
notes.back: At creation: it drives handling requirements in every later phase.
notes.extra: K8s: destroy = crypto-shredding, PV reclaim policy Delete.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.text: Sanitization: {{c1::clearing}}: logical overwrite, defeats ordinary recovery tools; {{c2::purging}}: degauss/secure erase, defeats lab recovery; {{c3::destruction}}: physical (shred, incinerate).

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.front: What is crypto-erasure, and why is it the practical purge in cloud?
notes.back: Encrypt the data, then destroy the key. You can't shred a provider's disks, so delete the customer-managed key.
notes.analogy: Throwing the only key to a safe into the ocean: the safe still exists, but nobody can open it.
notes.extra: Watch remanence in forgotten etcd snapshots and registry layers.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.text: Data states and protections: at rest → {{c1::storage encryption (AES)}}; in transit → {{c2::TLS / IPsec}}; in use → {{c3::memory protection, confidential computing (TEEs)}}.
notes.extra: K8s: etcd KMS encryption (rest), mTLS or WireGuard (transit), AMD SEV / Intel TDX node pools (use).

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.front: Scoping vs tailoring a baseline?
notes.back: Scoping: choose which controls apply (drop irrelevant ones). Tailoring: adjust the remaining ones to the organization (parameters, compensating controls). Document both.
notes.extra: K8s: scoping BIO2 to a platform: "physical media → provider responsibility".

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.text: {{c1::Data residency}} = where data is physically stored; {{c2::data sovereignty}} = data is subject to the laws where it resides (and possibly the provider's home country); {{c3::data localization}} = a legal requirement to keep data in a jurisdiction.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.front: Why does the US CLOUD Act matter when choosing an EU cloud?
notes.back: US providers can be compelled to disclose data even when it is stored in the EU, so residency doesn't guarantee sovereignty.
notes.extra: This drives EU sovereign-cloud choices in public-sector procurement.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.front: Why is asset inventory foundational to security?
notes.back: You can't protect what you don't know exists. Inventory (with owner and classification) underpins vulnerability management, incident response and audits.
notes.extra: K8s: Git = intended state, cluster API = actual state; ArgoCD OutOfSync drift is a detective control.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.front: What does Data Loss Prevention (DLP) do?
notes.back: Detects and blocks unauthorized exfiltration of sensitive data using classification labels, patterns or fingerprints.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::02 Asset Security
notes.front: Network DLP vs endpoint DLP? Where does a CASB fit?
notes.back: Network: inspects data in motion at egress. Endpoint: controls copy/print/USB on hosts. A CASB extends DLP to SaaS.
notes.extra: K8s: egress NetworkPolicies/gateways limit where data can flow.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.text: Bell-LaPadula protects {{c1::confidentiality}}: no read {{c2::up}} (simple security property), no write {{c3::down}} (* property).
notes.analogy: A spy can't read files above their clearance, and can't leak secrets by writing them into a lower-level file.
notes.extra: Strong star: read/write only at your own level. Ignores integrity.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.text: Biba protects {{c1::integrity}}: no read {{c2::down}} (simple integrity), no write {{c3::up}} (* integrity). It is the inverse of Bell-LaPadula.
notes.analogy: A careful scientist won't cite tabloids (read down) and won't let interns edit the peer-reviewed journal (write up).
notes.extra: K8s: prod (high integrity) must not pull from unvetted registries; dev pipelines must not push to the prod registry project.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.text: Clark-Wilson enforces integrity through {{c1::well-formed transactions}} and {{c2::separation of duties}}; users reach data only through programs (the access triple user → TP → CDI).
notes.analogy: A bank ledger: customers never write in it directly; only tellers' audited transactions can change it.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.text: Clark-Wilson elements: {{c1::CDIs}} (constrained data items) may be changed only by {{c2::TPs}} (transformation procedures); {{c3::IVPs}} (integrity verification procedures) check CDIs are valid; UDIs are unconstrained input.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: How is GitOps an instance of Clark-Wilson?
notes.back: Cluster state = CDI; PR + review + pipeline = TP; author ≠ reviewer = separation of duties; ArgoCD drift check = IVP.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: What problem does Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall) solve, and how?
notes.back: Conflicts of interest: once a subject accesses one company's data, access to competitors' data in the same class is blocked (rights change dynamically).
notes.extra: K8s: hard tenant isolation (separate clusters/node pools) when serving competitors.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: What is a reference monitor?
notes.back: The abstract mechanism that mediates every subject→object access to enforce policy. Implemented by the security kernel within the TCB.
notes.analogy: A single security desk that every visitor must pass, every time, with no side doors.
notes.extra: K8s: the API server's authn → authz → admission chain approximates one for cluster state.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.text: A reference monitor must be {{c1::tamper-proof}}, {{c2::always invoked (non-bypassable)}} and {{c3::small enough to verify}}.
notes.extra: K8s: "always invoked" is why direct etcd access, kubelet APIs and node SSH must be locked down.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.text: Saltzer & Schroeder: {{c1::complete mediation}}: check every access, every time; {{c2::open design}}: security mustn't depend on a secret design; {{c3::economy of mechanism}}: keep it small and simple.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: "Fail securely" in Kubernetes: what do webhook failurePolicy: Fail vs Ignore mean?
notes.back: Fail = fail closed (secure; deploys blocked if the webhook is down). Ignore = fail open (available, unenforced).
notes.analogy: A bank vault that locks during a power cut (fail closed) vs a fire exit that unlocks (fail open).

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: Symmetric vs asymmetric cryptography: main strength and weakness of each?
notes.back: Symmetric (AES, ChaCha20): fast; key distribution is hard. Asymmetric (RSA, ECC): solves distribution and enables signatures; slow.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.text: Key counts: {{c1::n(n−1)/2}} symmetric keys for n users to talk pairwise, vs {{c2::2n}} keys (one pair each) with asymmetric crypto.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: How does hybrid cryptography work, e.g. in TLS?
notes.back: Asymmetric crypto (ECDHE key exchange, certificates) establishes a symmetric session key; bulk data is encrypted symmetrically.
notes.analogy: Send a padlocked box by mail to agree on a shared key once, then talk freely using that key.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.text: Hash → {{c1::integrity}} only; HMAC → integrity + {{c2::authenticity}}; digital signature → integrity + authenticity + {{c3::non-repudiation}}.
notes.extra: K8s: pin image digests (@sha256:…) for integrity; a cosign signature adds authenticity.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: Why doesn't an HMAC provide non-repudiation?
notes.back: Both parties share the secret key, so either could have produced the MAC.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: What is envelope encryption?
notes.back: Data is encrypted with a local DEK; the DEK is encrypted (wrapped) by a KEK that never leaves the KMS/HSM.
notes.analogy: Your house key sits in a lockbox; only the lockbox key lives in the bank vault.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: Why is envelope encryption standard in cloud KMS design?
notes.back: Bulk data never goes to the KMS, the KEK stays in hardened storage, and rotating the KEK only re-wraps DEKs.
notes.extra: K8s: etcd KMS encryption: one DEK per Secret, wrapped by the cloud KEK.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: In a PKI, Certificate Authority vs Registration Authority?
notes.back: CA: issues and signs certificates (X.509, binding identity to public key). RA: verifies the requester's identity first.
notes.extra: Root CAs stay offline; online intermediates issue.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: CRL vs OCSP?
notes.back: CRL: a periodically published list of revoked certs. OCSP: a real-time query for one cert's status.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: Why do cloud-native PKIs favour short-lived certificates over revocation?
notes.back: A cert valid for hours expires before revocation would propagate, so lifetime replaces CRL/OCSP.
notes.extra: K8s: cert-manager automates renewal; SPIFFE/SPIRE issues short-lived workload SVIDs.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: VM vs container: isolation boundary?
notes.back: VMs: hardware-virtualized, separate kernels; strong boundary. Containers: share the host kernel; one kernel exploit escapes all containers on the node.
notes.extra: K8s: untrusted tenants → gVisor/Kata RuntimeClass, dedicated node pools or separate clusters.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: TPM vs HSM?
notes.back: TPM: a chip on the board storing keys and boot measurements for one machine. HSM: a dedicated tamper-resistant device for key storage and crypto at scale (FIPS 140).
notes.extra: Cloud KMS services keep KEKs in HSMs.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::03 Security Architecture & Engineering
notes.front: Secure boot vs measured boot?
notes.back: Secure boot: each stage verifies the next one's signature and refuses unsigned code. Measured boot: each stage is hashed into TPM PCRs for later attestation.
notes.extra: K8s: node attestation verifies a node's measurements before it joins.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: OSI layers bottom-up, with a mnemonic?
notes.back: Physical, Data Link, Network, Transport, Session, Presentation, Application: "Please Do Not Throw Sausage Pizza Away".

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: At which OSI layers do NetworkPolicy and Ingress controllers / service meshes operate?
notes.back: NetworkPolicy: L3/L4 (IP, port). Ingress and meshes: L7 (HTTP paths, identities).
notes.extra: The layer tells you what a control can see.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.text: TCP/IP ↔ OSI: link ↔ OSI {{c1::1–2}}; internet ↔ OSI {{c2::3}}; transport ↔ OSI 4; application ↔ OSI {{c3::5–7}}.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: What does mutual TLS add over standard TLS?
notes.back: The client also presents a certificate, so both sides are cryptographically authenticated: machine-to-machine auth without shared secrets.
notes.extra: K8s: meshes (Istio, Linkerd) give each pod a SPIFFE identity and enforce mTLS transparently.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: Microsegmentation vs traditional segmentation?
notes.back: Traditional: coarse zones (VLANs, subnets, DMZ), perimeter-focused. Micro: per-workload, identity-based east-west policy that assumes breach.
notes.analogy: Traditional segmentation locks the building's floors; microsegmentation locks every office door.
notes.extra: K8s: NetworkPolicy default-deny per namespace, then allow by label.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.text: Firewall types: {{c1::packet-filtering}}: stateless header rules; {{c2::stateful}}: tracks connections; {{c3::application-layer proxy}}: understands protocols, terminates connections; NGFW adds identity/IPS; {{c4::WAF}}: HTTP-specific (SQLi, XSS).
notes.extra: Cloud: security groups ≈ stateful L3/L4; Ingress + ModSecurity/Coraza ≈ WAF.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.text: IPsec: {{c1::AH}} gives integrity and origin authentication but no encryption; {{c2::ESP}} gives encryption (plus integrity); {{c3::IKE}} negotiates keys.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: IPsec VPN vs TLS VPN?
notes.back: IPsec: network-layer tunnel, the site-to-site standard. TLS VPN: runs over TCP 443, firewall-friendly, common for remote users.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: What distinguishes WireGuard, and where do Kubernetes CNIs use it?
notes.back: A minimal-codebase L3 VPN with fixed modern crypto (small attack surface). Cilium/Calico use it for transparent node-to-node pod traffic encryption.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: What is DNS cache poisoning, and what is the main defense?
notes.back: Forged responses cached by a resolver redirect victims. DNSSEC signs records so resolvers can verify them.
notes.extra: K8s: CoreDNS is critical: restrict who can change its config via RBAC.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: DNSSEC vs DoH/DoT: what does each protect?
notes.back: DNSSEC: integrity and authenticity of answers, not confidentiality. DoH/DoT: encrypt queries for privacy.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: What is DNS tunneling, and how do you detect it?
notes.back: Exfiltration or C2 hidden in DNS queries/responses. Detect unusual query volume, long or high-entropy names.
notes.extra: K8s: Cilium DNS-aware egress policies allow only expected names.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: Zero trust: the three main tenets?
notes.back: Verify explicitly (every request, all signals); least-privilege access (just-in-time, just-enough); assume breach (segment, encrypt, monitor).
notes.analogy: An airport where every gate scans your boarding pass again, rather than trusting you because you got past the entrance.
notes.extra: K8s: SPIFFE + mTLS, namespace-scoped RBAC, default-deny NetworkPolicies, Falco.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: NAT vs PAT, and what does egress NAT mean for allowlisting pod traffic?
notes.back: NAT maps private ↔ public addresses; PAT puts many hosts behind one IP using ports. External systems see the node/NAT-gateway IP, so allowlist there, not per pod.
notes.extra: Per-workload identity needs an egress gateway.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::04 Communication & Network Security
notes.front: What is SDN, and what's its main security risk?
notes.back: Separating a central, API-driven control plane from the forwarding data plane. Risk: the controller is a high-value single point of compromise.
notes.extra: K8s: the CNI controller programs every node; compromising it or its RBAC = owning the network.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.text: IAAA: {{c1::identification}}: claim an identity; {{c2::authentication}}: prove it; {{c3::authorization}}: what it may do; {{c4::accountability}}: tie actions to identities via audit trails.
notes.extra: K8s: OIDC tokens/client certs → RBAC → API-server audit log to a SIEM.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.text: Authentication factors: Type 1 = something you {{c1::know}}; Type 2 = something you {{c2::have}}; Type 3 = something you {{c3::are}}.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: Why is password + security question not MFA?
notes.back: Both are "something you know": MFA requires factors from different categories.
notes.extra: K8s: use an OIDC IdP with phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2), not long-lived kubeconfig certs.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.text: {{c1::SAML}}: XML-based authentication federation (enterprise SSO); {{c2::OAuth 2.0}}: authorization delegation with access tokens; {{c3::OIDC}}: an authentication layer on OAuth 2.0 using JWT ID tokens.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: Why isn't OAuth 2.0 alone an authentication protocol?
notes.back: Its access token says what a client may do, not who the user is; OIDC adds the ID token with identity claims.
notes.analogy: OAuth is a hotel key card: it opens doors but doesn't say who is holding it. OIDC adds the passport.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: How does the Kubernetes API server use OIDC?
notes.back: It validates IdP-issued ID tokens; the groups claim maps to RBAC bindings, so one IdP gives one MFA policy and one deprovisioning point.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.text: Access control models: {{c1::RBAC}}: permissions bundled into roles; {{c2::ABAC}}: policy evaluates subject, object and environment attributes; {{c3::rule-based}}: uniform rules for everyone (e.g. firewall ACLs).

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: DAC vs MAC?
notes.back: DAC: the owner decides access (e.g. chmod). MAC: system-wide labels/clearances the owner can't override.
notes.extra: Linux: file permissions are DAC; SELinux/AppArmor add MAC on top via the LSM framework.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: Kubernetes RBAC is additive only. How do you express a deny?
notes.back: Not in RBAC. Use admission policy (ValidatingAdmissionPolicy, Kyverno, OPA) for ABAC-style deny rules.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: Least privilege vs need to know?
notes.back: Least privilege: minimum permissions (actions). Need to know: access to specific information only when required.
notes.analogy: A valet key starts the car but won't open the boot: least privilege limits actions; need to know limits which boxes you can open.
notes.extra: K8s: namespaced Roles over ClusterRoles; per-namespace External Secrets stores = need to know for secrets.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: What is privilege creep, and what control counters it?
notes.back: Rights accumulating as people change roles without old access being removed. Counter: periodic access reviews.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: In privileged access management, why prefer just-in-time elevation to standing privileges?
notes.back: Time-boxed, approved, recorded elevation shrinks the window in which a stolen admin credential is useful.
notes.extra: K8s: no standing cluster-admin; expiring IdP group membership or Teleport with session recording.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: What is a break-glass account, and how must it be handled?
notes.back: A sealed emergency credential (e.g. for IdP outage); its use is heavily logged, alarmed and reviewed afterwards.
notes.analogy: The fire-alarm box behind glass: anyone can use it in an emergency, but breaking it sets off alarms.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: How should non-human (machine) identities be handled?
notes.back: Like humans: a unique identity per workload, least privilege, short-lived credentials instead of static secrets, rotation and audit.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: What is workload identity federation?
notes.back: Exchanging a workload's short-lived platform token for cloud credentials, so no static cloud keys live in the cluster.
notes.extra: K8s: projected ServiceAccount tokens → IRSA / GCP Workload Identity.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.text: Kerberos: the {{c1::KDC}} = Authentication Server + Ticket-Granting Server. Login yields a {{c2::TGT}}, which is exchanged for {{c3::service tickets}} per resource.
notes.analogy: A festival wristband (TGT) that you swap at each tent for a single-ride token (service ticket).
notes.extra: Port 88. Symmetric-key SSO.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: Why does Kerberos require synchronized clocks?
notes.back: Tickets and authenticators carry timestamps to prevent replay; skew beyond a few minutes makes authentication fail.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: What is Kerberos' biggest architectural weakness?
notes.back: The KDC: it holds every principal's key, so its compromise is total compromise (and a single point of failure).

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: In the joiner–mover–leaver lifecycle, which stage most causes privilege creep, and why?
notes.back: Mover: new rights are added but old ones aren't removed.
notes.extra: Best practice: HR-driven automated provisioning.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: What is access recertification?
notes.back: Periodic review where data owners confirm each user's access is still needed.
notes.extra: K8s: with RBAC in Git and access via one IdP, review = git log + group audit.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: Main security benefits of SSO?
notes.back: Fewer passwords, strong central authentication (MFA once), central deprovisioning and better audit.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::05 Identity & Access Management
notes.front: Main risk of SSO, and mitigations?
notes.back: The IdP is a single point of failure and "keys to the kingdom": one stolen session unlocks everything. Mitigate: short token lifetimes, phishing-resistant MFA, a break-glass path.
notes.analogy: A master key: convenient for the owner, catastrophic if copied.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::06 Security Assessment & Testing
notes.front: Vulnerability assessment vs penetration test?
notes.back: Assessment: breadth-first automated scanning for known weaknesses, no exploitation. Pen test: depth-first authorized exploitation showing real impact and chains; needs written rules of engagement.
notes.extra: K8s: kube-bench/Trivy = assessment; SA-token theft → privesc → node escape = pen test.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::06 Security Assessment & Testing
notes.text: SOC reports: {{c1::SOC 1}} = controls relevant to financial reporting; {{c2::SOC 2}} = Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, privacy), restricted distribution; {{c3::SOC 3}} = public summary of SOC 2.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::06 Security Assessment & Testing
notes.front: SOC 2 Type I vs Type II?
notes.back: Type I: control design at a point in time. Type II: operating effectiveness over a period (6–12 months), much stronger assurance.
notes.analogy: Type I is a photo of the guard at the gate; Type II is six months of CCTV showing he was always there.
notes.extra: How you assess a cloud provider you can't audit: SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, C5.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::06 Security Assessment & Testing
notes.text: Test knowledge levels: {{c1::black-box}}: no internal knowledge (external attacker); {{c2::gray-box}}: partial knowledge (insider / post-breach); {{c3::white-box}}: full source and config access (most thorough).
notes.extra: K8s: gray-box: give a tester one low-privilege SA token and see how far they get.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::06 Security Assessment & Testing
notes.text: {{c1::SAST}}: analyses source without running it; {{c2::DAST}}: probes the running app from outside; {{c3::SCA}}: inventories dependencies and their CVEs; {{c4::IAST}}: instruments the running app from inside.
notes.extra: K8s: SAST + secret scan on commit → SCA/image scan at build → DAST on preview env.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::06 Security Assessment & Testing
notes.text: Audits: {{c1::internal}}: own staff, for management; {{c2::external}}: independent firm hired by the organization; {{c3::third-party}}: mandated by an outside authority (regulator, customer).
notes.extra: Your job in a regulatory audit: auditable evidence mapping policy to technical controls.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::06 Security Assessment & Testing
notes.front: What are synthetic transactions?
notes.back: Scripted actions run continuously against a live system to verify behaviour and performance before users notice failures.
notes.extra: K8s: blackbox-exporter probes, scheduled canary login.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::06 Security Assessment & Testing
notes.front: What is misuse-case testing?
notes.back: Testing what the system must not allow: the negative counterpart of use-case testing.
notes.extra: K8s: a CI job tries to deploy an unsigned image or privileged pod and fails the build if the platform permits it.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::06 Security Assessment & Testing
notes.text: DR test types, by rising risk: {{c1::read-through / checklist}} → {{c2::structured walk-through (tabletop)}} → {{c3::simulation}} → {{c4::parallel}} → {{c5::full interruption}}.
notes.extra: K8s: restore Velero backups into a scratch cluster to measure real RTO (simulation).

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::06 Security Assessment & Testing
notes.front: KPI vs KRI in a security program?
notes.back: KPI: how well controls perform now (patch latency, MTTD). KRI: forward-looking early warning that risk is rising.
notes.extra: K8s: KRI: growth in cluster-admin bindings, count of policy exceptions.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.text: (ISC)² incident steps: detection → {{c1::response}} → {{c2::mitigation (containment)}} → reporting → recovery → {{c3::remediation (root cause)}} → lessons learned.
notes.extra: K8s: Falco alert → cordon node, quarantine NetworkPolicy → NIS2 24 h warning → redeploy from Git → fix image + admission rule.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.text: NIST SP 800-61 IR phases: preparation → {{c1::detection & analysis}} → {{c2::containment, eradication & recovery}} → post-incident activity.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.front: SIEM vs SOAR?
notes.back: SIEM: aggregates and correlates logs, raises alerts. SOAR: runs playbooks on those alerts (enrich, contain, ticket).
notes.analogy: SIEM is the smoke detector panel; SOAR is the sprinkler system wired to it.
notes.extra: K8s: feed the SIEM API audit logs and Falco events; a SOAR playbook applies a quarantine NetworkPolicy.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.text: Order of volatility (collect first → last): {{c1::CPU registers/cache}} → {{c2::RAM (processes, network state)}} → disk → logs/backups → archival media.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.front: What is chain of custody?
notes.back: A documented, unbroken record of who handled evidence, when and how; required for admissibility. Hash evidence at collection.
notes.analogy: A sealed evidence bag with a signature log of every hand it passed through.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.front: In a container incident, why not delete the compromised pod first?
notes.back: Its memory and ephemeral filesystem vanish. Isolate it (NetworkPolicy), capture memory/artifacts and snapshot the node, then terminate.
notes.extra: Off-node centralized logs are the durable evidence.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.text: Backups: {{c1::full}}: everything, fastest restore; {{c2::incremental}}: changes since the last backup of any kind, restore = full + every incremental; {{c3::differential}}: changes since the last full, restore = full + latest differential.
notes.extra: Archive bit: full and incremental clear it; differential doesn't.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.text: The 3-2-1 backup rule: {{c1::3}} copies, on {{c2::2}} different media, {{c3::1}} offsite.
notes.extra: K8s: with GitOps, Git holds desired state; only data and secrets need classic backup.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.text: RAID: {{c1::0}} = striping, no redundancy; {{c2::1}} = mirroring; {{c3::5}} = striping + single parity (survives 1 disk); {{c4::6}} = double parity (survives 2); 10 = mirrored stripes.
notes.extra: Ceph/Longhorn apply the same ideas across nodes and zones.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.text: DR sites: {{c1::hot}}: fully equipped, near-current data, RTO minutes–hours; {{c2::warm}}: equipment ready, data restored on activation, RTO hours–days; {{c3::cold}}: space and power only, RTO days–weeks.
notes.extra: K8s: a GitOps "pilot-light" cluster gives warm cost with near-hot RTO.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.front: What security purpose does change management serve?
notes.back: A request → approve → test → implement → review cycle stops unauthorized or unvetted changes and leaves an audit trail.
notes.extra: K8s: GitOps: PR = request, review = approval, CI = test, merge = implement.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.front: What does configuration management add to change management?
notes.back: Known-good baselines plus detection and correction of drift from them.
notes.extra: K8s: ArgoCD drift detection + self-heal.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.front: Patch management lifecycle?
notes.back: Identify → evaluate/prioritize (risk-based: CVSS + exploitability) → test → deploy → verify.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.front: How does immutable infrastructure change patching?
notes.back: Never patch in place: build a new image and replace the instance.
notes.analogy: You don't repair a paper cup, you take a fresh one.
notes.extra: K8s: rolling node-pool upgrades; rebuild images on base updates; Trivy Operator rescans running images.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.front: Application allowlisting vs denylisting: which is stronger, and why?
notes.back: Allowlisting (default deny): novel malware is blocked by default. Denylisting only blocks known bad. Cost: allowlists need upkeep.
notes.extra: K8s: Kyverno allows only approved registries and signed images.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.text: Availability ≈ {{c1::MTBF}} / (MTBF + {{c2::MTTR}}).
notes.extra: MTBF = mean time between failures; MTTR = mean time to repair. Declarative redeploy from Git shrinks MTTR.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.text: Incident-response speed metrics: {{c1::MTTD}} = mean time to detect; {{c2::MTTC}} = mean time to contain.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::07 Security Operations
notes.front: Threat hunting vs alert-driven monitoring?
notes.back: Hunting is proactive and hypothesis-driven, looking for adversaries that didn't trigger alerts (often structured by MITRE ATT&CK). Monitoring reacts to alerts.
notes.extra: K8s: hunt for exec into prod pods or SA tokens used from unexpected IPs.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: Why is integrating security early in the SDLC ("shift left") economical?
notes.back: Defects cost orders of magnitude more to fix in production than in design, so threat modeling and testing go into every phase.
notes.extra: K8s: threat model → pre-commit secret scan → SAST/SCA → signed artifacts → admission policy → runtime detection.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: Waterfall vs Agile vs DevSecOps: where does security fit?
notes.back: Waterfall: phase gates, late feedback. Agile: must be in the definition of done or it's skipped. DevSecOps: automated, embedded controls in the pipeline.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: How does separation of duties survive in DevOps?
notes.back: As enforced pipeline controls: protected branches, mandatory review, signed artifacts and no human write access to production.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: Why is the CI/CD pipeline a high-value target, and what are its key controls?
notes.back: It holds deploy credentials and produces trusted artifacts. Controls: hardened, isolated runners; scoped short-lived tokens; protected branches + review; signed, attested artifacts.
notes.extra: K8s: Tekton Chains signs builds and emits SLSA provenance; admission verifies it.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: What is the canonical defense against injection (OWASP Top 10)?
notes.back: Parameterized queries / prepared statements plus input validation; never build queries by string concatenation.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: Why is SSRF especially dangerous in cloud and Kubernetes?
notes.back: The server can be tricked into calling internal endpoints, such as the cloud metadata service, and leaking instance credentials.
notes.extra: Mitigate: IMDSv2 / metadata blocking via egress NetworkPolicy.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: What is an SBOM, and what question does it answer fast?
notes.back: A machine-readable inventory of an artifact's components (SPDX, CycloneDX). It answers "are we exposed?" when a new CVE drops (cf. Log4Shell).
notes.analogy: The ingredients label on food: when a contaminated ingredient is recalled, you check labels instead of testing every jar.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: What is SLSA?
notes.back: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts: a build-integrity maturity framework. Build levels 1–3 climb from documented provenance to signed provenance from a hardened build platform.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: A secret was committed to Git. What is the fix?
notes.back: Rotate it. Deleting the commit isn't enough: clones, forks, caches and history keep it.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: How do GitOps setups keep secrets out of Git?
notes.back: Fetch at runtime from a secret manager (External Secrets Operator + Vault/cloud store), or commit only encrypted forms (Sealed Secrets, SOPS).
notes.extra: Plus gitleaks in pre-commit and CI.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.text: CMMI levels: 1 {{c1::initial}} → 2 {{c2::managed}} → 3 {{c3::defined}} → 4 {{c4::quantitatively managed}} → 5 {{c5::optimizing}}.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: OWASP SAMM vs BSIMM?
notes.back: SAMM: prescriptive, open framework telling you how to mature. BSIMM: descriptive benchmark of what other organizations actually do.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: What risks does acquired software (COTS, open source) bring, and which controls apply?
notes.back: Imported vulnerabilities, licences and maintenance risk. Controls: supplier assessment, SCA, licence compliance, SBOM in contracts, project-health monitoring.
notes.extra: xz-utils (2024): a socially engineered maintainer. Pin digests, verify provenance, use minimal images.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: What is BOLA, the top API flaw?
notes.back: Broken Object-Level Authorization: the API doesn't check that the caller may access this object ID, so changing /orders/123 to /124 leaks data.

notes.deck: CISSP (Cloud & Kubernetes Grounded)::08 Software Development Security
notes.front: Which controls does an API gateway centralize, and what keeps it from being bypassed?
notes.back: TLS termination, JWT validation, rate limits and per-route authorization. NetworkPolicies make backends reachable only through the gateway (complete mediation).
